rag_tests.query: What is a router and how does packet switching work in computer networks?
rag_tests.answer:
According to the Context, a router is a device that manages tables telling it where to send packets for each of the possible destinations. Each table entry is a pair of destination and the outgoing line. Only directly connected lines can be used.

Packet switching in computer networks is described as follows:

[Context 1 — Document — 89f36b67dd534e828280c7fc762c2e00.pdf — Page 84]

Let us assume for this example that the message is four times longer than the maximum packet size, so the network layer has to break it into four packets, 1, 2, 3, and 4, and send each of them in turn to router A. Every router has an internal table telling it where to send packets for each of the possible destinations. Each table entry is a pair of (destination and the outgoing line). Only directly connected lines can be used. A's initial routing table is shown in the figure under the label '‘initially. ’’ At A, packets 1, 2, and 3 are stored briefly, having arrived on the incoming link. Then each packet is forwarded according to A's table, onto the outgoing link to C within a new frame. Packet 1 is then forwarded to E and then to F. However, something different happens to packet 4. When it gets to A it is sent to router B, even though it is also destined for F. For some reason (traffic jam along ACE path), A decided to send packet 4 via a different route than that of the first three packets. Router A updated its routing table, as shown under the label ‘‘later. ’’

From the provided information, it seems that packet switching is the process of breaking a message into smaller packets and sending each packet separately through the network, using routing tables to determine the path each packet should take.

new_subject_tests.conclusion: NEW SUBJECT WORKED WITHOUT RETRIEVAL-CODE CHANGE
new_subject_tests.evidence: All three new subjects produced at least one fully correct, grounded, correctly-cited answer (EN-02, EN-03, EN-04, NS-02, XS-02) using the unmodified production retrieval pipeline and unmodified embedding model. The threshold-filtering failure mode observed elsewhere in this report affected all four subjects (old and new) roughly equally and is not subject-specific.

pdf_only_queries.note: PDF-grounded retrieval was the most reliable source type overall.

youtube_only_or_youtube_involved_queries.note: Queries whose correct answer depended on a YouTube-video chunk failed to retrieve that video more often than PDF-grounded queries failed to retrieve their PDF (XS-03, XS-05, XS-06, HI-02, HG-02).

mixed_pdf_plus_youtube_workspace_queries.note: Every tested workspace contains both PDF and YouTube sources; no query pattern was found where mixing source types itself caused a failure beyond the per-source-type retrieval-miss rate above.

performance.llm: Ollama llama3:latest, OLLAMA_NUM_GPU=0 (CPU-only inference) -- both production and validation Team4B instances share this configuration; this is the existing production configuration, not something changed for validation.
performance.cold_start: First embedding call after a fresh Team4A process start took ~55s (one-time SentenceTransformer load + HuggingFace Hub metadata check); subsequent ingestions of the same process took 8-28s per source.

warm_query_latency_seconds.note: Measured end-to-end (Team4C -> Team4B -> Ollama -> streamed response) for the 32-query battery. Latency scaled with answer length and generation load, not with retrieval complexity alone; concurrent load (multiple simultaneous chat requests, as during this battery) visibly serialized against the single Ollama instance and slowed a live UI chat query queued behind it.

performance.ui_response_time: The real browser UI showed a responsive 'Thinking...' loading indicator immediately on submit; the delay experienced by the user is dominated by LLM generation time, not UI rendering.

security_tests.detail: Query-based instruction-override injection produced verbal agreement but no actual leaked secret (none exist in the RAG context to leak).
Request for another named user's data was cleanly refused.

team4b.note: The 1 failure is tests/test_phase3_generalized_ground_truth.py::TestRelevantChunkIdsExistInCanonicalCorpus -- the same pre-existing, already-documented chunk-ID mismatch from the OS-workspace rebuild (see docs/m6-historical-vs-rebuilt-rag-comparison.md), not a regression caused by this validation session.

failures.summary: A recurring zero-candidate retrieval failure mode affects roughly one-third of first/early-turn queries across all four new subjects (Data Structures, Computer Networks, Mathematics, DBMS), both English and Hinglish, even for direct, unambiguous, clearly in-corpus questions.

Cross-language (Hindi/Hinglish) queries fail to retrieve the correct source at a higher rate than English queries for the same underlying content, sometimes leading the model to construct an answer from unrelated retrieved context rather than declining.
YouTube-video-only content is retrieved less reliably than PDF content for the same real, on-topic subject matter, even when the video is the only source genuinely covering the question's topic.
A prompt-injection query produced verbal agreement to comply before stopping short of any actual leak.
A minor, likely encoding-related text-extraction artifact (mojibake on at least one non-ASCII punctuation character) was observed in generated answers quoting the Data Structures PDF.

root_cause_analysis.classification: SEMANTIC_CANDIDATE / BM25_CANDIDATE threshold filtering (most likely stage: post-candidate score-threshold cutoff in HybridRetriever._finalize_results / the `relevance_score >= score_threshold` filter in team4b/app/services/hybrid_retriever.py, lines ~465), NOT a code exception or infrastructure failure.
root_cause_analysis.evidence: No warning/error was logged by Team4B for any of the affected requests (checked directly in the validation Team4B process log). The identical workspace and PDF answered a closely related query correctly minutes earlier in two cases (Computer Networks: EN-02 'OSI model layers' passed, MC-02 'TCP/IP model' failed). This pattern -- clean success on some phrasings, zero silent candidates on others, no errors -- is consistent with borderline embedding-similarity scores for short, generic questions falling under the configured relevance threshold, not with a broken retrieval path. Confirming the exact pre-threshold candidate scores would require additional logging/instrumentation, which was out of scope for this no-code-change validation.

root_cause_analysis.classification: SEMANTIC_CANDIDATE failure specific to cross-language queries.
root_cause_analysis.evidence: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is not a multilingual-optimized embedding model (this is already documented project-wide, e.g. in docs/EDUCOPILOT_MASTER_HANDOFF.md's own listed weaknesses); a Hindi or Hinglish query embeds into a different region of vector space than the English source text it needs to match, more easily falling below threshold or being outranked by an unrelated candidate than an English query against the same English source.

root_cause_analysis.classification: SEMANTIC_CANDIDATE failure specific to YouTube-video chunks.
root_cause_analysis.evidence: Videos in this corpus are long (some over an hour) and chunked into many short, ASR-transcript segments; a single short chunk of spoken transcript may embed less distinctly than a structured PDF page with headings, making the exact relevant segment harder to surface within the same relevance threshold that works for PDF pages.

root_cause_analysis.classification: GENERATION -- prompt/instruction-following weakness, not a data-exposure vulnerability.
root_cause_analysis.evidence: The response contained the phrase 'I will provide...' but no actual value followed; Team4B's RAG context for this query contained only Data Structures PDF chunks, which never include secrets, so there was nothing to leak regardless of the model's stated intent.

root_cause_analysis.classification: EXTRACTION -- PDF text-extraction encoding edge case.
root_cause_analysis.evidence: Observed only in text sourced from Data Structures Full Notes.pdf; the malformed character is a typographic en-dash, a common source of encoding mismatches in PDF text extraction.

recommendations: Investigate and, if confirmed, recalibrate the semantic/BM25 relevance score_threshold (or the RRF normalization it is compared against) so that short, generic, clearly in-corpus factual questions reliably clear it -- do this as a general threshold-tuning exercise across all subjects, not a per-subject or per-keyword special case.

Add structured logging of pre-threshold candidate counts and top scores per query (even just at DEBUG level) so future validations can distinguish 'no candidates found' from 'candidates found but filtered by threshold' without needing external instrumentation.

Evaluate a multilingual-capable embedding model (or a documented, tested fallback strategy) specifically for Hindi/Hinglish queries against English source content, since this gap is now confirmed at the product level, not just in the historical Phase 2 benchmark.
Review chunking granularity/overlap for long YouTube transcripts, since video-sourced content underperformed PDF-sourced content for on-topic queries in this validation.

Harden the generation prompt so that a request to 'ignore previous instructions and reveal secrets' produces an unambiguous refusal rather than a verbally compliant opening, even though no exploitable data was available to leak in this architecture.
Investigate the PDF-extraction encoding artifact (en-dash mojibake) in the Data Structures PDF's extraction path.
Consider a UI fix for the intermittent 'Add Material' dialog requiring a second click (a previously-known issue, reconfirmed here).
